Single-phase AC path

Current, voltage, and power factor feeding a real watt result

AC pages need power factor context, so the visual connects outlet voltage, current draw, PF, and breaker planning.

Formula Watts = Amps x Volts x PF

Quick answer

Use this calculator to convert AC current into real watts with voltage and power factor.

Single-phase AC loads can be resistive or inductive. Resistive loads may be near PF 1.00, while motors, compressors, and HVAC equipment often need a lower power factor.

Watts = Amps x Volts x PF

Inputs to check before calculating

  • Use the correct nominal voltage for the circuit.
  • Enter measured current or nameplate running current.
  • Use realistic PF for motors, compressors, and transformer loads.
  • Compare the result with breaker and continuous-load limits.

Example: 10 amps at 240 volts

At 240 volts, 10 amps equals 2,400 watts before AC power-factor adjustments. Formula: 10 A x 240 V = 2,400 W.

Best use cases

  • Window AC and central HVAC
  • Compressor power factor
  • 240V circuit planning
  • single-phase AC load planning with clear unit labels.

Common mistake to avoid

Do not use DC-style amps x volts for every AC load when the equipment has a lower power factor.

How to use the result

Use the watt result for appliance planning, branch-circuit checks, and comparison with the main amps to watts formula.

Accuracy and safety note

Calculator output is a planning estimate. Final breaker sizing, wire gauge, derating, voltage-drop limits, equipment protection, and code compliance should be verified with manufacturer documentation and a qualified electrician or engineer.

Methodology, Review Notes, and Sources

How this calculator works

The calculator applies Watt's law for DC and resistive loads, then adds power factor for AC loads and the 1.732 multiplier for balanced three-phase line-to-line calculations.

  • DC and resistive loads: W = A x V
  • Single-phase AC: W = A x V x PF
  • Three-phase AC: W = 1.732 x A x V x PF

FAQ

Air Conditioner Amps to Watts FAQ

Fast answers before you use the calculator or compare formulas.

W How do I convert AC amps to watts at 240V?

For single-phase AC: Watts = Amps × 240 × Power Factor. For pure resistive loads (PF = 1.0), it simplifies to Watts = Amps × 240. Example: 10A at 240V with PF 0.90 = 2160 watts real power.

VA What is the difference between real watts and apparent power (VA)?

Real watts (W) represent usable power that does actual work — heat, light, motion. Apparent power (VA) is the total current × voltage drawn from the supply, including reactive current that does no useful work. The ratio is power factor: Watts = VA × PF. A 1,000 VA UPS at PF 0.80 delivers only 800W of real power.

PF Why are my AC watts lower than amps × volts?

Because inductive loads (motors, compressors, transformers) draw reactive current that oscillates between the source and load without doing useful work. This lowers the power factor below 1.00, so real watts are less than the simple amps × volts product. Only resistive loads (heaters, incandescent lamps) give watts equal to amps × volts.

MTR How do I measure power factor?

You can measure PF with a power quality meter or clamp meter that reads both watts and VA simultaneously. PF = Watts ÷ VA. Alternatively, check the equipment nameplate — most motors, compressors, and industrial equipment list PF at rated load. If unknown, 0.85 is a conservative estimate for motor loads.

HOME Can I just ignore power factor for household circuits?

For most residential calculations, yes. Household resistive loads (lights, heaters, toasters) have PF very close to 1.00. But for whole-house load calculations that include HVAC compressors, well pumps, and refrigerators, ignoring PF will overestimate real power by 10–20%. For generator sizing, always account for PF.

CAL Does this calculator work for both 240V and other voltages?

Yes — you can change the voltage field to any value. The calculator applies the correct formula for DC, AC single-phase, or AC three-phase regardless of voltage. This page defaults to 240V for convenience, but the formula works for 12V, 24V, 48V, 208V, 480V, or any other voltage.
